query:
We are designing a small, research-grade (desktop) laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for screening new aluminium alloys made in-house in small batches (a few hundred grams of ultrasonically atomized powder per alloy, 15-63 um). Please review the peer-reviewed literature (and theses / HardwareX / open-hardware papers where available) on the DESIGN and CUSTOMIZATION of LPBF systems, and give quantitative design values with citations for each of the following:

1. Open-source and open-architecture LPBF machines and custom research testbeds (e.g. NIST AMMT, university-built LPBF testbeds, low-cost or open-hardware LPBF builds, Aconity-type open platforms, miniaturized or reduced-build-volume LPBF for alloy screening). What laser, scanner, chamber, recoater and gas system did each use, what did it cost, and what lessons did the builders report?
2. Powder spreading: blade vs. roller (rotating, counter-rotating) vs. compliant/brush recoaters; recoater speed, gap and layer thickness; spreadability metrics and their dependence on particle size distribution and morphology; designs that minimise powder consumption (small build plate, build-plate inserts, dose-on-demand or reduced-volume feed, powder supply from above vs. piston feed).
3. Inert-gas environment: achievable and required O2 levels (ppm) for Al alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc/Zr), purge strategies (vacuum-purge-backfill vs. flow-through), cross-flow velocity across the plate for plume/spatter removal, nozzle and outlet design, filtration, gas consumption, and O2/H2O sensing.
4. Beam delivery: galvanometer scanner + f-theta lens vs. XY-gantry-moved optics (or hybrid gantry + galvo) for LPBF; achievable scan speeds and accelerations, effects of gantry acceleration/jerk on track quality, spot size (50-100 um) and focal-shift considerations, fiber laser power (200-500 W at 1070 nm) and its suitability for aluminium (reflectivity), protective window contamination.
5. Controls and electronics: scanner protocols (XY2-100, SL2-100), laser modulation and synchronisation with motion, open-source control software, in-situ monitoring (coaxial photodiode/pyrometer, layer cameras) used in custom LPBF machines.
6. Safety: laser safety for Class 4 enclosed systems (ANSI Z136.1, IEC 60825-1/-4, interlocks, laser-safe viewing windows), combustible/reactive metal powder handling for aluminium (NFPA 484, wet separators, filter passivation, PPE), and incidents or hazards reported in research LPBF labs.

Please end with a ranked list of the design choices most supported by the literature for a sub-$60k custom desktop LPBF machine optimised for good spreadability, safety, ease of automation, smooth motion, minimal powder (hopper) volume and high-purity inert gas.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation

        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment

    ObservationalModel:

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: We are designing a small, research-grade (desktop) laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for screening new aluminium alloys made in-house in small batches (a few hundred grams of ultrasonically atomized powder per alloy, 15-63 um). Please review the peer-reviewed literature (and theses / HardwareX / open-hardware papers where available) on the DESIGN and CUSTOMIZATION of LPBF systems, and give quantitative design values with citations for each of the following:

1. Open-source and open-architecture LPBF machines and custom research testbeds (e.g. NIST AMMT, university-built LPBF testbeds, low-cost or open-hardware LPBF builds, Aconity-type open platforms, miniaturized or reduced-build-volume LPBF for alloy screening). Abstract:
This paper presents a real-time geometry-informed control strategy to homogenize melt pool measurements in laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) using reinforcement learning. The learning control strategy incorporates geometric information of the scan path as well as in-situ melt pool measurements to compute the laser power signal for reducing in-process melt pool inhomogeneities. First, we design and validate a data-driven model to train the reinforcement learning agent in simulation, with the goal of reducing the amount of experimental data needed for training. Using this simulation-based training approach has the added benefit of avoiding unsafe or infeasible experiments, an issue that is often encountered in training the reinforcement learning agent. After training, the learned control strategy attenuates the 1-norm error by 37% and standard deviation by 39% in simulation. We then deploy this learned control strategy in an experimental test bed for a new scan geometry. In this test scenario, the policy achieves a 30% reduction in error, and a 36% reduction in melt pool signal variation, thereby illustrating the potential of reinforcement learning in real-time geometry-agnostic control for L-PBF. Finally, we demonstrate that the reinforcement learning agent delivers the same level of performance as a model-based feedforward controller with PID feedback, with $20\times $ less computational time for a single geometry. Note to Practitioners—This work was motivated by the need to develop a practical control algorithm for L-PBF systems. Because L-PBF systems manufacture customized on-demand geometries, it is critical that the control strategy is extendable to and easily optimized for each geometry. Specifically, this effort develops an efficient and robust reinforcement learning control algorithm that can be used across novel part geometries, once trained. The control strategy is designed using a simulation-to-real approach, which is key for avoiding extensive training effort and avoids unsafe training experiments.

Abstract:
Powder bed fusion—laser beam (PBF-LB), a prevalent and rapidly advancing additive manufacturing (AM) technology nowadays, serves the industry by producing thin, complex, and lightweight components for various sectors, including healthcare, automotive, defence, and aerospace. However, this technology encounters challenges related to the construction of critical parts and the high overall process costs. Equally significant is the role of support structures in metal laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M). The absence of supports can lead to defective and collapsed parts, while the incorrect selection of a support type or the addition of unnecessary supports results in increased material usage and additional post-processing efforts. Therefore, there is a pressing need for advanced software capable of generating appropriate support structures and predicting the thermomechanical behaviour of a part under PBF-LB/M printing conditions. Such software would be beneficial for the industry to avoid printing defects caused by high thermal stresses, minimise material usage, reduce printing time, and ensure high-quality prints. In this study, we introduce a web-based support generation and optimisation platform for PBF-LB/M. Through this platform, among other features, users can import three-dimensional (3D) parts and generate block-type support structures with diamond perforations based on the PySLM library, all within a user-friendly web environment. The first release of the platform (v0.6) is fully interactive and accessible online at no cost.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing is an emerging 3D printing technique for the fabrication of advanced metal components. Widespread adoption of it and similar additive technologies is hampered by poor understanding of laser-metal interactions under such extreme thermal regimes. Here, we elucidate the mechanism of pore formation and liquid-solid interface dynamics during typical laser powder bed fusion conditions using in situ X-ray imaging and multi-physics simulations. Pores are revealed to form during changes in laser scan velocity due to the rapid formation then collapse of deep keyhole depressions in the surface which traps inert shielding gas in the solidifying metal. We develop a universal mitigation strategy which eliminates this pore formation process and improves the geometric quality of melt tracks. Our results provide insight into the physics of laser-metal interaction and demonstrate the potential for science-based approaches to improve confidence in components produced by laser powder bed fusion. Laser-matter interactions during laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing remain poorly understood. Here, the authors combine in situ X-ray imaging and finite element simulations to show how detrimental pores form under printing conditions and develop a strategy to suppress them.

The Use of Miniature Specimens to Determine Local Properties and Fracture Behavior of LPBF-Processed Inconel 718 in as-Deposited and Post-Treated States Valid Text Names: 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 1-2', 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 2-4', 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 4-11', 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 11-12', 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 12-18', 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 18-19', 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 19-20' BibTex: @article{dzugan2022theuseof, author = "Dzugan, Jan and Seifi, Mohsen and Rund, Martin and Podany, Pavel and Grylls, Richard and Lewandowski, John J.", title = "The Use of Miniature Specimens to Determine Local Properties and Fracture Behavior of LPBF-Processed Inconel 718 in as-Deposited and Post-Treated States", year = "2022", journal = "Materials", volume = "15", pages = "4724", month = "Jul", doi = "10.3390/ma15134724", url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/ma15134724", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "13", issn = "1996-1944" } Abstract: This paper summarizes the assessment of directional anisotropy in local mechanical properties for Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) IN-718 bulk samples via the use of miniature samples excised from the bulk for both as-deposited and post-treated states. The quasi-static tensile properties at room temperature are investigated at several different locations along the build direction and at different orientations for both considered states. A comparison between the excised miniature tensile specimens and standard-sized sample results have also been conducted and exhibit very good agreement. Significant anisotropy is present in mechanical properties at different build heights for the as-deposited state, while the post-treated material exhibited more homogenous properties, both along the height and for different sampling orientations. However, significant reductions (e.g., >30%) in the strength (Yield, UTS) along with a significant increase in the reduction in area at fracture is found for post-processed materials. Metallography and fractography analyses were conducted in order to begin to determine the source(s) of this anisotropy for the as-deposited state. Rapid Alloy Development of Extremely High-Alloyed Metals Using Powder Blends in Laser Powder Bed Fusion Valid Text Names: 'ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment pages 1-3', 'ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment pages 3-6', 'ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment pages 6-11', 'ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment pages 11-12', 'ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment pages 12-14', 'ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment pages 14-15' BibTex: @article{ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment, author = "Ewald, Simon and Kies, Fabian and Hermsen, Steffen and Voshage, Maximilian and Haase, Christian and Schleifenbaum, Johannes Henrich", title = "Rapid Alloy Development of Extremely High-Alloyed Metals Using Powder Blends in Laser Powder Bed Fusion", year = "2019", journal = "Materials", volume = "12", pages = "1706", month = "May", doi = "10.3390/ma12101706", url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/ma12101706", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "10", issn = "1996-1944" } Abstract: The design of new alloys by and for metal additive manufacturing (AM) is an emerging field of research. Currently, pre-alloyed powders are used in metal AM, which are expensive and inflexible in terms of varying chemical composition. The present study describes the adaption of rapid alloy development in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) by using elemental powder blends. This enables an agile and resource-efficient approach to designing and screening new alloys through fast generation of alloys with varying chemical compositions. This method was evaluated on the new and chemically complex materials group of multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs). MPEAs constitute ideal candidates for the introduced methodology due to the large space for possible alloys. First, process parameters for LPBF with powder blends containing at least five different elemental powders were developed. Secondly, the influence of processing parameters and the resulting energy density input on the homogeneity of the manufactured parts were investigated. Microstructural characterization was carried out by optical microscopy, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), while mechanical properties were evaluated using tensile testing. Finally, the applicability of powder blends in LPBF was demonstrated through the manufacture of geometrically complex lattice structures with energy absorption functionality. Laser Powder-Bed Fusion as an Alloy Development Tool: Parameter Selection for In-Situ Alloying Using Elemental Powders Valid Text Names: 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 1-3', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 3-4', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 4-7', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 7-10', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 10-12', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 12-15', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 15-16', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 16-17' BibTex: @article{aota2020laserpowderbedfusion, author = "Aota, Leonardo Shoji and Bajaj, Priyanshu and Sandim, Hugo Ricardo Zschommler and Jägle, Eric Aimé", title = "Laser Powder-Bed Fusion as an Alloy Development Tool: Parameter Selection for In-Situ Alloying Using Elemental Powders", year = "2020", journal = "Materials", volume = "13", pages = "3922", month = "Sep", doi = "10.3390/ma13183922", url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/ma13183922", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "18", issn = "1996-1944" } Abstract: The design of advanced alloys specifically tailored to additive manufacturing processes is a research field that is attracting ever-increasing attention. Laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) commonly uses pre-alloyed, fine powders (diameter usually 15–45 µm) to produce fully dense metallic parts. The availability of such fine, pre-alloyed powders reduces the iteration speed of alloy development for LPBF and renders it quite costly. Here, we overcome these drawbacks by performing in-situ alloying in LPBF starting with pure elemental powder mixtures avoiding the use of costly pre-alloyed powders. Pure iron, chromium, and nickel powder mixtures were used to perform in-situ alloying to manufacture 304 L stainless steel cube-shaped samples. Process parameters including scanning speed, laser power, beam diameter, and layer thickness were varied aiming at obtaining a chemically homogeneous alloy. The scientific questions focused on in this work are: which process parameters are required for producing such samples (in part already known in the state of the art), and why are these parameters conducive to homogeneity? Analytical modelling of the melt pool geometry and temperature field suggests that the residence time in the liquid state is the most important parameter controlling the chemical homogeneity of the parts. Results show that in-situ alloying can be successfully employed to enable faster and cost-efficient rapid alloy development. Exploring the fabrication limits of thin-wall structures in a laser powder bed fusion process Valid Text Names: 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 1-2', 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 2-4', 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 4-5', 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 5-7', 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 7-8', 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 8-10', 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 10-13', 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 13-15', 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 15-16', 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 16-17', 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 17-17' BibTex: @article{wu2020exploringthefabrication, author = "Wu, Ziheng and Narra, Sneha Prabha and Rollett, Anthony", title = "Exploring the fabrication limits of thin-wall structures in a laser powder bed fusion process", year = "2020", journal = "The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology", volume = "110", pages = "191-207", month = "Aug", doi = "10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4", url = "https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", issue = "1-2", issn = "0268-3768" } Abstract: Although additive manufacturing (AM) is becoming increasingly popular for various applications, few studies have addressed design and potential problems in thin wall fabrication for the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process. In the LPBF process, rapid cooling induces thermal shrinkage, which in turn, results in high residual stress and complicates thin wall fabrication. The minimum wall thickness is limited by the parameters and machine settings while the dimensional accuracy is controlled by the powder size, scan strategy, and part geometry. The ability to fabricate thin-wall components is important for applications such as heat exchangers (HX). This study explores the performance of the LPBF process by fabricating thin walls with extreme geometries in different processing conditions and alloys using an EOS M290 LPBF machine. Results show that the material, part design, and scanning strategy contribute to the variation in thin wall dimensions. A maximum inclination angle of 60° and a minimum wall thickness of ~ 100 μm in Ti-6Al-4V, Inconel 718, and AlSi10Mg were achieved using optimized part design and processing conditions. The effects of part design and material on the thermal distortion and surface finish of thin walls were also investigated leading to a discussion on how the scan mode assigned by the EOS software affects design and fabrication. Additionally, synchrotron-based X-ray micro-tomography (μSXCT) was utilized to quantify the porosity in thin-wall structures and to correlate it with the integrity of the structures. Comprehensive design guidelines presented in this work can increase the success rate of fabricating thin-wall geometries. A critical review on the effects of process-induced porosity on the mechanical properties of alloys fabricated by laser powder bed fusion Valid Text Names: 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 1-3', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 3-6', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 6-8', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 8-11', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 11-15', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 15-17', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 17-18', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 18-20', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 20-21', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 21-25', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 25-28', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 28-30', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 30-32', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 32-34', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 34-36', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 36-37', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 37-38', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 38-40', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 40-41', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 41-42', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 42-44', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 44-45', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 45-46', 'kan2022acriticalreview pages 46-48' BibTex: @article{kan2022acriticalreview, author = "Kan, Wen Hao and Chiu, Louis Ngai Sam and Lim, Chao Voon Samuel and Zhu, Yuman and Tian, Yang and Jiang, Derui and Huang, Aijun", title = "A critical review on the effects of process-induced porosity on the mechanical properties of alloys fabricated by laser powder bed fusion", year = "2022", journal = "Journal of Materials Science", volume = "57", pages = "9818-9865", month = "Mar", doi = "10.1007/s10853-022-06990-7", url = "https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-022-06990-7", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", issue = "21", issn = "0022-2461" } Abstract: Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is an emerging additive manufacturing technique that is currently adopted by a number of industries for its ability to directly fabricate complex near-net-shaped components with minimal material wastage. Two major limitations of LPBF, however, are that the process inherently produces components containing some amount of porosity and that fabricated components tend to suffer from poor repeatability. While recent advances have allowed the porosity level to be reduced to a minimum, consistent porosity-free fabrication remains elusive. Therefore, it is important to understand how porosity affects mechanical properties in alloys fabricated this way in order to inform the safe design and application of components. To this aim, this article will review recent literature on the effects of porosity on tensile properties, fatigue life, impact and fracture toughness, creep response, and wear behavior. As the number of alloys that can be fabricated by this technology continues to grow, this overview will mainly focus on four alloys that are commonly fabricated by LPBF—Ti-6Al-4 V, Inconel 718, AISI 316L, and AlSi10Mg. Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is an additive manufacturing technique whose efficiency and quality depend largely on a consistent and precise powder spreading procedure. This article examines the crucial role of powder spreading in influencing the quality of 3D-printed parts. Through case studies and experimental results, the article demonstrates in detail the impact of parameters such as: powder flowability, spreading speed, layer thickness, and recoater type on powder uniformity during spreading. In addition, the paper presents a comparison between types of recoaters in order to obtain optimum surface finish, mechanical properties, and reduced defects. This paper reviews the most appropriate powder spreading techniques to maintain the flowability and uniformity of the powder. Therefore, the primary objective of this work is to present an in-depth review of the impact of powder spreading dynamics in LPBF. In addition, it aims to demonstrate to the reader the various factors influencing powder spreading and the methodologies employed to optimize this crucial process.

Abstract:
Powder bed fusion (PBF), a subset of additive manufacturing methods, is well known for its promise in the production of fully functional artefacts with high densities. The quality of the powder bed, commonly referred to as powder spreading, is a crucial determinant of the final quality of the produced artefact in the PBF process. Therefore, it is critical that we examine the factors that impact the powder spreading, notably the powder bed quality. This study utilised a newly developed testing apparatus, designed specifically for examining the quality of powder beds. The objective was to analyse the influence of various factors, including the recoater shape, recoater gap size, and the different powder flow properties, on the powder bed relative packing fraction. Additionally, the study aimed to assess the variation in the particle size and shape across the build plate. The results indicated that all of the variables examined had an impact on the relative packing fraction, as well as the size and shape variations observed across the build plate.

Abstract:
Shielding gas flow is essential to the additive manufacturing (AM) process, and the effects of argon shielding gas flow variation on the macroscopic homogeneity of additive manufactured stainless steel parts have been studied using an open-architecture AM system. Such a variation manifests itself layer-by-layer within one part and part-by-part across the build plate. Within one build, a combination of balling behavior, conduction melting and keyhole melting is observed across the build plate using the same laser parameters. Quantitative characterization of the melt pool shapes show that the melt pool width and the penetration depth exhibit the largest variations. Possible relations between the gas flow condition and macroscopic structure variations are discussed and guidelines for improved design of a gas flow system as well as future research directions are suggested for achieving macroscopically uniform metal AM.

Abstract:
Laser processing is a versatile tool that enhances smart materials for diverse industries, allowing precise changes in material properties and customization of surface characteristics. It drives the development of smart materials with adaptive properties through laser modification, utilizing photothermal reactions and functional additives for meticulous control. These laser-processed smart materials form the foundation of 4D printing that enables dynamic shape changes depending on external influences, with significant potential in the aerospace, robotics, health care, electronics, and automotive sectors, thus fostering innovation. Laser processing also advances photonics and optoelectronics, facilitating precise control over optical properties and promoting responsive device development for various applications. The application of computer-generated diffractive optical elements (DOEs) enhances laser precision, allowing for predetermined temperature distribution and showcasing substantial promise in enhancing smart material properties. This comprehensive overview explores the applications of laser technology and nanotechnology involving DOEs, underscoring their transformative potential in the realms of photonics and optoelectronics. The growing potential for further research and practical applications in this field suggests promising prospects in the near future.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) and direct laser deposition (DLD) are the two main processes currently used in the additive manufacturing (AM) of metals. For both methods, metal powders are used as feedstock, and they must present specific physical and chemical properties to ensure optimal processing and reliable and reproducible printing results. Particle morphology, size distribution, and flowability, among other factors, depend on the powder production process and directly influence the processing parameters and physical characteristics of the parts built by AM. This systematic review presents different concepts involving L-PBF and DLD manufacturing and the application of metal powders. The methods used to produce and characterize metal powders and the modification techniques to improve their processability by AM are detailed and discussed. Environmental and health risks are also presented, and safety measures that must be considered while handling metal powders. Some key topics requiring attention for further development are highlighted. Graphical abstract

Abstract:
The additive manufacturing process creates objects directly by stacking layers of material on each other until the required product is obtained. The application of additive manufacturing technology for teaching and research purposes is still limited and unpopular in developing countries, due to costs and lack of accessibility. In this study, an extruding-based 3D printing additive manufacturing technology was employed to design and construct a low-cost-high-accessibility 3D printing machine to manufacture plastic objects. The machine was designed using SolidWorks 2020 version with a 10 × 10 × 10 cm3 build volume. The fabrication was carried out using locally available materials, such as PVC pipes for the frame, plywood for the bed, and Zinc Oxide plaster for the bed surface. Repetier firmware was the operating environment for devices running on the computer operating system. Cura was used as the slicing software. The fabricated machine was tested, and the printer produced 3D components with desired structural dimensions. The fabricated 3D printer was used to manufacture some plastic objects using PLA filament. The recommended distance between the nozzle tip and the bed is 0.1 mm. The constructed 3D printer is affordable and accessible, especially in developing nations where 3D printing applications are limited and unpopular.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of titanium or titanium alloys allows fabrication of geometrically more complex and, possibly, individualized implants or osteosynthesis products and could thus improve the outcome of medical treatments considerably. However, insufficient LPBF process parameters can result in substantial porosity, decreasing mechanical properties and requiring post-treatment. Furthermore, texturized parts with anisotropic properties are usually obtained after LPBF processing, limiting their usage in medical applications. The present study addresses both: first, a design of experiments is used in order to establish a set of optimized process parameters and a process window for LPBF printing of small commercially pure (CP) titanium parts with minimized volume porosity. Afterward, the first results on the development of a biocompatible titanium alloy designed for LPBF processing of medical implants with improved solidification and more isotropic properties are presented on the basis of conventionally melted alloys. This development was performed on the basis of Ti-0.44O-0.5Fe-0.08C-0.4Si-0.1Au, a near-α alloy presented by the authors for medical applications and conventional manufacturing, with yttrium and boron additions as additional growth restriction solutes. In terms of LPBF processing of CP titanium grade 1 powder, a high relative density of approximately 99.9% was obtained in the as-printed state of the volume of a small cubical sample by using optimized laser power, scanning speed, and hatch distance in combination with a rotating scanning pattern. Moreover, tensile specimens processed with these volume settings and tested in the as-printed milled state exhibited a high average yield and ultimate tensile strength of approximately 663 and 747 N/mm2, respectively, combined with a high average ductility of approximately 24%. X-ray diffraction results suggest anisotropic mechanical properties, which are, however, less pronounced in terms of the tested specimens. Regarding alloy development, the results show that yttrium additions lead to a considerable microstructure refinement but have to be limited due to the occurrence of a large amount of precipitations and a supposed higher propensity for the formation of long columnar prior β-grains. However, phase/texture and microstructure analyses indicate that Ti-0.44O-0.5Fe-0.08C-0.4Si-0.1Au-0.1B-0.1Y is a promising candidate to achieve lower anisotropy during LPBF processing, but further investigations on LPBF printing and Y2O3 formation are necessary.

Abstract:
The growing demand for more materials available for the LPBF-process, in particular high-strength aluminum alloys, is evident in the market. In the present work, a systematic investigation of the processability of aluminum 6182 series alloys, using LPBF, was carried out. For this purpose, the influence of process parameters, especially of enhanced preheating by heating the substrate plate during the LPBF process, on the microstructure of EN AW 6182 specimens was studied. Experiments were conducted at different preheating temperatures always using the same d-optimal design-of-experiments, the laser power, scanning speed, hatch distance, and laser focus position being varied over a wide range. It was found that the preheating temperature has the strongest impact on hot cracking. Higher temperatures result in a significantly reduced number of hot cracks in the microstructure. Moreover, an equiaxed microstructure of the specimens manufactured can be observed at preheating temperatures of 500 °C. In addition to the preheating temperature, the achievable part density is most strongly affected by the laser focus position and the laser power, whereas the hatch distance shows no discernible impact on the part density. Furthermore, neither the hatch distance nor the laser focus position shows any significant effect on hot cracking. In combination with the optimal scanning parameters, crack-free parts with a fully equiaxed grain structure and densities > 99.0% can be manufactured via LPBF at a preheating temperature of 500 °C.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) is a layerwise production process that creates three-dimensional objects according to a digital model. This technology has demonstrated to be a promising alternative to conventional manufacturing methods for various industrial sectors, such as aerospace, automotive, biomedical, and energy. AM offers several advantages, like design flexibility, material efficiency, functional integration, and rapid prototyping. As regards metal parts, conventional AM techniques using infrared laser sources face some limitations in processing high-reflectivity and high-conductivity materials or alloys, such as aluminum, copper, gold, and silver. These materials have low absorption of infrared radiation, which results in unstable and shallow melt pools, poor surface quality, and high porosity. To overcome these challenges, green and blue laser sources have been proposed for AM processes. This review provides an overview of the recent developments and applications of green and blue laser sources for powder bed fusion of copper and its alloys, focusing on the effects of process parameters on the melt pool dynamics, microstructure formation, and thermal and electrical properties of the fabricated parts. This review also presents the main applications of AM of copper and its alloys together with potential opportunities for future developments.

The excerpt describes an open-architecture DTU LPBF controller centered on a Teensy 3.6 with a 180 MHz ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller. It uses direct memory access (DMA), timer interrupts, and a circular command buffer so scanner and laser operation can continue while commands are received and processed. The scanner interface is the XY2-100 protocol: a 20-bit, 2 MHz asynchronous digital protocol using four differential pairs for clock, synchronization, and two mirror-position data channels. Each control word contains three mode bits, 16 position bits, and a parity bit; the galvanometer system therefore provides a 16-bit-by-16-bit discrete position space. Bresenham line approximation is used for incremental scanner motion. The controller supports laser power and duty-cycle ramping within a single command, including ramping from 0 to 250 W and back, and supports continuous or pulsed operation such as 1 kHz at 80% duty cycle. For process monitoring, it provides three configurable sensor inputs accepting 0–10 V or 4–20 mA signals, with sensors for oxygen, gas flow, pressure, and light intensity. The NIST powder spreading testbed (PST) is a compact, two-axis powder-spreading apparatus intended to reproduce key aspects of commercial laser powder bed fusion while reducing powder requirements and fitting inside an environmentally controlled chamber. Powder heaps are generated either with a stencil, which is convenient for single-layer spreading and creates a narrower heap, or with a rotating steel-cylinder apparatus, which is better suited to multilayer spreading but produces a more distributed heap. The excerpt does not provide quantitative definitions or measurement procedures for spreadability metrics such as coverage, packing fraction, or surface roughness. The excerpt describes a bespoke MIT/Hart LPBF testbed developed for aperture-division-multiplexing (ADM) monitoring. A key mechanical constraint is that the distance between the main build plate and enclosure lid is limited to 60 mm, which constrains the working distance of both laser-delivery and monitoring optics while still allowing powder recoating. The enclosure is designed so the top does not need to be removed during operation; monitoring optics attach to mounting features on the lid and can remain installed after focusing and alignment. Build-plate installation and part removal are performed from the front. The machine includes a build piston, piston-fed powder supply, and compliant-blade recoating mechanism, with these functions actuated by industrial-automation-grade servo motors. The laser scan head is suspended on a boom above the enclosure and delivers light from a 500 W, 1.075 µm SPI redPOWER qube single-mode fiber laser. The laser has 82 mrad beam divergence and is paired with a 250 mm collimator, producing a 19.5 mm beam diameter. The excerpt does not provide specific scanner hardware, detailed monitoring performance, or system cost. It indicates that the monitoring setup is intended to support ADM-based optical process monitoring.

The excerpt provides only partial design information about the MIT/Hart bespoke LPBF testbed. The process laser is a 500 W, 1.075 µm SPI redPOWER qube single-mode fiber laser. Its 82 mrad divergence is combined with a 250 mm collimator, producing an approximately 19.5 mm diameter beam, and a Thorlabs QS20XY galvanometer performs laser scanning. Machine operation is automated through an NI-cRIO-9039 on a 10 µs timebase. A layer cycle includes powder spreading, gas-knife activation two seconds before fusion, synchronized laser/galvanometer operation, and a further two-second gas-knife period before recoating; the gas-knife signal also triggers the camera and suppresses data collection during recoating. Optical monitoring uses a bespoke aperture-division-multiplexing lens shared by the laser-delivery and imaging paths. The system provides approximately 50 µm imaging resolution and high temporal resolution with a high-speed MWIR camera. The IRCameras IRC806HS has a 640 × 512 InSb detector sensitive from 1–5 µm, with 20 µm pixels, and is connected through Camera-Link cables and an NI frame grabber. The excerpt does not specify the build piston, powder-supply mechanism, recoater type, enclosure construction beyond an environmental enclosure and protective calcium-fluoride window, or system cost.

function.name: create_artifact

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
