info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: We are designing a small, research-grade (desktop) laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for screening new aluminium alloys made in-house in small batches (a few hundred grams of ultrasonically atomized powder per alloy, 15-63 um). Please review the peer-reviewed literature (and theses / HardwareX / open-hardware papers where available) on the DESIGN and CUSTOMIZATION of LPBF systems, and give quantitative design values with citations for each of the following:

1. Open-source and open-architecture LPBF machines and custom research testbeds (e.g. NIST AMMT, university-built LPBF testbeds, low-cost or open-hardware LPBF builds, Aconity-type open platforms, miniaturized or reduced-build-volume LPBF for alloy screening). What laser, scanner, chamber, recoater and gas system did each use, what did it cost, and what lessons did the builders report?
2. Powder spreading: blade vs. roller (rotating, counter-rotating) vs. compliant/brush recoaters; recoater speed, gap and layer thickness; spreadability metrics and their dependence on particle size distribution and morphology; designs that minimise powder consumption (small build plate, build-plate inserts, dose-on-demand or reduced-volume feed, powder supply from above vs. piston feed).
3. Inert-gas environment: achievable and required O2 levels (ppm) for Al alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc/Zr), purge strategies (vacuum-purge-backfill vs. flow-through), cross-flow velocity across the plate for plume/spatter removal, nozzle and outlet design, filtration, gas consumption, and O2/H2O sensing.
4. Beam delivery: galvanometer scanner + f-theta lens vs. XY-gantry-moved optics (or hybrid gantry + galvo) for LPBF; achievable scan speeds and accelerations, effects of gantry acceleration/jerk on track quality, spot size (50-100 um) and focal-shift considerations, fiber laser power (200-500 W at 1070 nm) and its suitability for aluminium (reflectivity), protective window contamination.
5. Controls and electronics: scanner protocols (XY2-100, SL2-100), laser modulation and synchronisation with motion, open-source control software, in-situ monitoring (coaxial photodiode/pyrometer, layer cameras) used in custom LPBF machines.
6. Safety: laser safety for Class 4 enclosed systems (ANSI Z136.1, IEC 60825-1/-4, interlocks, laser-safe viewing windows), combustible/reactive metal powder handling for aluminium (NFPA 484, wet separators, filter passivation, PPE), and incidents or hazards reported in research LPBF labs.

Please end with a ranked list of the design choices most supported by the literature for a sub-$60k custom desktop LPBF machine optimised for good spreadability, safety, ease of automation, smooth motion, minimal powder (hopper) volume and high-purity inert gas.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this multi-faceted question about designing a custom desktop LPBF machine for aluminum alloy screening.

## 5. Real-Time Melt Pool Homogenization Through Geometry-Informed Control in Laser Powder Bed Fusion Using Reinforcement Learning
Valid Text Names:

    year = "2025",

Abstract:
This paper presents a real-time geometry-informed control strategy to homogenize melt pool measurements in laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) using reinforcement learning. The learning control strategy incorporates geometric information of the scan path as well as in-situ melt pool measurements to compute the laser power signal for reducing in-process melt pool inhomogeneities. First, we design and validate a data-driven model to train the reinforcement learning agent in simulation, with the goal of reducing the amount of experimental data needed for training. Using this simulation-based training approach has the added benefit of avoiding unsafe or infeasible experiments, an issue that is often encountered in training the reinforcement learning agent. After training, the learned control strategy attenuates the 1-norm error by 37% and standard deviation by 39% in simulation. We then deploy this learned control strategy in an experimental test bed for a new scan geometry. In this test scenario, the policy achieves a 30% reduction in error, and a 36% reduction in melt pool signal variation, thereby illustrating the potential of reinforcement learning in real-time geometry-agnostic control for L-PBF. Finally, we demonstrate that the reinforcement learning agent delivers the same level of performance as a model-based feedforward controller with PID feedback, with $20\times $ less computational time for a single geometry. Note to Practitioners—This work was motivated by the need to develop a practical control algorithm for L-PBF systems. Because L-PBF systems manufacture customized on-demand geometries, it is critical that the control strategy is extendable to and easily optimized for each geometry. Specifically, this effort develops an efficient and robust reinforcement learning control algorithm that can be used across novel part geometries, once trained. The control strategy is designed using a simulation-to-real approach, which is key for avoiding extensive training effort and avoids unsafe training experiments.

Abstract:
Powder bed fusion—laser beam (PBF-LB), a prevalent and rapidly advancing additive manufacturing (AM) technology nowadays, serves the industry by producing thin, complex, and lightweight components for various sectors, including healthcare, automotive, defence, and aerospace. However, this technology encounters challenges related to the construction of critical parts and the high overall process costs. Equally significant is the role of support structures in metal laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M). The absence of supports can lead to defective and collapsed parts, while the incorrect selection of a support type or the addition of unnecessary supports results in increased material usage and additional post-processing efforts. Therefore, there is a pressing need for advanced software capable of generating appropriate support structures and predicting the thermomechanical behaviour of a part under PBF-LB/M printing conditions. Such software would be beneficial for the industry to avoid printing defects caused by high thermal stresses, minimise material usage, reduce printing time, and ensure high-quality prints. In this study, we introduce a web-based support generation and optimisation platform for PBF-LB/M. Through this platform, among other features, users can import three-dimensional (3D) parts and generate block-type support structures with diamond perforations based on the PySLM library, all within a user-friendly web environment. The first release of the platform (v0.6) is fully interactive and accessible online at no cost.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing is an emerging 3D printing technique for the fabrication of advanced metal components. Widespread adoption of it and similar additive technologies is hampered by poor understanding of laser-metal interactions under such extreme thermal regimes. Here, we elucidate the mechanism of pore formation and liquid-solid interface dynamics during typical laser powder bed fusion conditions using in situ X-ray imaging and multi-physics simulations. Pores are revealed to form during changes in laser scan velocity due to the rapid formation then collapse of deep keyhole depressions in the surface which traps inert shielding gas in the solidifying metal. We develop a universal mitigation strategy which eliminates this pore formation process and improves the geometric quality of melt tracks. Our results provide insight into the physics of laser-metal interaction and demonstrate the potential for science-based approaches to improve confidence in components produced by laser powder bed fusion. Laser-matter interactions during laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing remain poorly understood. Here, the authors combine in situ X-ray imaging and finite element simulations to show how detrimental pores form under printing conditions and develop a strategy to suppress them.

The Use of Miniature Specimens to Determine Local Properties and Fracture Behavior of LPBF-Processed Inconel 718 in as-Deposited and Post-Treated States Valid Text Names: 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 1-2', 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 2-4', 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 4-11', 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 11-12', 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 12-18', 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 18-19', 'dzugan2022theuseof pages 19-20' BibTex: @article{dzugan2022theuseof, author = "Dzugan, Jan and Seifi, Mohsen and Rund, Martin and Podany, Pavel and Grylls, Richard and Lewandowski, John J.", title = "The Use of Miniature Specimens to Determine Local Properties and Fracture Behavior of LPBF-Processed Inconel 718 in as-Deposited and Post-Treated States", year = "2022", journal = "Materials", volume = "15", pages = "4724", month = "Jul", doi = "10.3390/ma15134724", url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/ma15134724", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "13", issn = "1996-1944" } Abstract: This paper summarizes the assessment of directional anisotropy in local mechanical properties for Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) IN-718 bulk samples via the use of miniature samples excised from the bulk for both as-deposited and post-treated states. The quasi-static tensile properties at room temperature are investigated at several different locations along the build direction and at different orientations for both considered states. A comparison between the excised miniature tensile specimens and standard-sized sample results have also been conducted and exhibit very good agreement. Significant anisotropy is present in mechanical properties at different build heights for the as-deposited state, while the post-treated material exhibited more homogenous properties, both along the height and for different sampling orientations. However, significant reductions (e.g., >30%) in the strength (Yield, UTS) along with a significant increase in the reduction in area at fracture is found for post-processed materials. Metallography and fractography analyses were conducted in order to begin to determine the source(s) of this anisotropy for the as-deposited state. Rapid Alloy Development of Extremely High-Alloyed Metals Using Powder Blends in Laser Powder Bed Fusion Valid Text Names: 'ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment pages 1-3', 'ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment pages 3-6', 'ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment pages 6-11', 'ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment pages 11-12', 'ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment pages 12-14', 'ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment pages 14-15' BibTex: @article{ewald2019rapidalloydevelopment, author = "Ewald, Simon and Kies, Fabian and Hermsen, Steffen and Voshage, Maximilian and Haase, Christian and Schleifenbaum, Johannes Henrich", title = "Rapid Alloy Development of Extremely High-Alloyed Metals Using Powder Blends in Laser Powder Bed Fusion", year = "2019", journal = "Materials", volume = "12", pages = "1706", month = "May", doi = "10.3390/ma12101706", url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/ma12101706", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "10", issn = "1996-1944" } Abstract: The design of new alloys by and for metal additive manufacturing (AM) is an emerging field of research. Currently, pre-alloyed powders are used in metal AM, which are expensive and inflexible in terms of varying chemical composition. The present study describes the adaption of rapid alloy development in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) by using elemental powder blends. This enables an agile and resource-efficient approach to designing and screening new alloys through fast generation of alloys with varying chemical compositions. This method was evaluated on the new and chemically complex materials group of multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs). MPEAs constitute ideal candidates for the introduced methodology due to the large space for possible alloys. First, process parameters for LPBF with powder blends containing at least five different elemental powders were developed. Secondly, the influence of processing parameters and the resulting energy density input on the homogeneity of the manufactured parts were investigated. Microstructural characterization was carried out by optical microscopy, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), while mechanical properties were evaluated using tensile testing. Finally, the applicability of powder blends in LPBF was demonstrated through the manufacture of geometrically complex lattice structures with energy absorption functionality. Laser Powder-Bed Fusion as an Alloy Development Tool: Parameter Selection for In-Situ Alloying Using Elemental Powders Valid Text Names: 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 1-3', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 3-4', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 4-7', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 7-10', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 10-12', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 12-15', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 15-16', 'aota2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 16-17' BibTex: @article{aota2020laserpowderbedfusion, author = "Aota, Leonardo Shoji and Bajaj, Priyanshu and Sandim, Hugo Ricardo Zschommler and Jägle, Eric Aimé", title = "Laser Powder-Bed Fusion as an Alloy Development Tool: Parameter Selection for In-Situ Alloying Using Elemental Powders", year = "2020", journal = "Materials", volume = "13", pages = "3922", month = "Sep", doi = "10.3390/ma13183922", url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/ma13183922", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "18", issn = "1996-1944" } Abstract: The design of advanced alloys specifically tailored to additive manufacturing processes is a research field that is attracting ever-increasing attention. Laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) commonly uses pre-alloyed, fine powders (diameter usually 15–45 µm) to produce fully dense metallic parts. The availability of such fine, pre-alloyed powders reduces the iteration speed of alloy development for LPBF and renders it quite costly. Here, we overcome these drawbacks by performing in-situ alloying in LPBF starting with pure elemental powder mixtures avoiding the use of costly pre-alloyed powders. Pure iron, chromium, and nickel powder mixtures were used to perform in-situ alloying to manufacture 304 L stainless steel cube-shaped samples. Process parameters including scanning speed, laser power, beam diameter, and layer thickness were varied aiming at obtaining a chemically homogeneous alloy. The scientific questions focused on in this work are: which process parameters are required for producing such samples (in part already known in the state of the art), and why are these parameters conducive to homogeneity? Analytical modelling of the melt pool geometry and temperature field suggests that the residence time in the liquid state is the most important parameter controlling the chemical homogeneity of the parts. Results show that in-situ alloying can be successfully employed to enable faster and cost-efficient rapid alloy development. In the LPBF process, rapid cooling induces thermal shrinkage, which in turn, results in high residual stress and complicates thin wall fabrication. The minimum wall thickness is limited by the parameters and machine settings while the dimensional accuracy is controlled by the powder size, scan strategy, and part geometry. The ability to fabricate thin-wall components is important for applications such as heat exchangers (HX). This study explores the performance of the LPBF process by fabricating thin walls with extreme geometries in different processing conditions and alloys using an EOS M290 LPBF machine. Results show that the material, part design, and scanning strategy contribute to the variation in thin wall dimensions. The effects of part design and material on the thermal distortion and surface finish of thin walls were also investigated leading to a discussion on how the scan mode assigned by the EOS software affects design and fabrication. Additionally, synchrotron-based X-ray micro-tomography (μSXCT) was utilized to quantify the porosity in thin-wall structures and to correlate it with the integrity of the structures. Comprehensive design guidelines presented in this work can increase the success rate of fabricating thin-wall geometries. Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is an additive manufacturing technique whose efficiency and quality depend largely on a consistent and precise powder spreading procedure. This article examines the crucial role of powder spreading in influencing the quality of 3D-printed parts. Through case studies and experimental results, the article demonstrates in detail the impact of parameters such as: powder flowability, spreading speed, layer thickness, and recoater type on powder uniformity during spreading. In addition, the paper presents a comparison between types of recoaters in order to obtain optimum surface finish, mechanical properties, and reduced defects. This paper reviews the most appropriate powder spreading techniques to maintain the flowability and uniformity of the powder. Therefore, the primary objective of this work is to present an in-depth review of the impact of powder spreading dynamics in LPBF. In addition, it aims to demonstrate to the reader the various factors influencing powder spreading and the methodologies employed to optimize this crucial process.

Abstract:
Powder bed fusion (PBF), a subset of additive manufacturing methods, is well known for its promise in the production of fully functional artefacts with high densities. The quality of the powder bed, commonly referred to as powder spreading, is a crucial determinant of the final quality of the produced artefact in the PBF process. Therefore, it is critical that we examine the factors that impact the powder spreading, notably the powder bed quality. This study utilised a newly developed testing apparatus, designed specifically for examining the quality of powder beds. The objective was to analyse the influence of various factors, including the recoater shape, recoater gap size, and the different powder flow properties, on the powder bed relative packing fraction. Additionally, the study aimed to assess the variation in the particle size and shape across the build plate. The results indicated that all of the variables examined had an impact on the relative packing fraction, as well as the size and shape variations observed across the build plate.

Powder spreading is a crucial part of the LPBF AM process that defines the quality of the fabricated objects. In this study, the impacts of various input parameters on the spread of powder density and particle distribution during the powder spreading process are investigated using the DEM (discrete element method) simulation tool.     issue = "1",
    issn = "1757-8981"
}


Abstract:
Shielding gas flow is essential to the additive manufacturing (AM) process, and the effects of argon shielding gas flow variation on the macroscopic homogeneity of additive manufactured stainless steel parts have been studied using an open-architecture AM system. Such a variation manifests itself layer-by-layer within one part and part-by-part across the build plate. Within one build, a combination of balling behavior, conduction melting and keyhole melting is observed across the build plate using the same laser parameters. Quantitative characterization of the melt pool shapes show that the melt pool width and the penetration depth exhibit the largest variations. Possible relations between the gas flow condition and macroscopic structure variations are discussed and guidelines for improved design of a gas flow system as well as future research directions are suggested for achieving macroscopically uniform metal AM.

Abstract:
Laser processing is a versatile tool that enhances smart materials for diverse industries, allowing precise changes in material properties and customization of surface characteristics. It drives the development of smart materials with adaptive properties through laser modification, utilizing photothermal reactions and functional additives for meticulous control. These laser-processed smart materials form the foundation of 4D printing that enables dynamic shape changes depending on external influences, with significant potential in the aerospace, robotics, health care, electronics, and automotive sectors, thus fostering innovation. Laser processing also advances photonics and optoelectronics, facilitating precise control over optical properties and promoting responsive device development for various applications. The application of computer-generated diffractive optical elements (DOEs) enhances laser precision, allowing for predetermined temperature distribution and showcasing substantial promise in enhancing smart material properties. This comprehensive overview explores the applications of laser technology and nanotechnology involving DOEs, underscoring their transformative potential in the realms of photonics and optoelectronics. The growing potential for further research and practical applications in this field suggests promising prospects in the near future.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) and direct laser deposition (DLD) are the two main processes currently used in the additive manufacturing (AM) of metals. For both methods, metal powders are used as feedstock, and they must present specific physical and chemical properties to ensure optimal processing and reliable and reproducible printing results. Particle morphology, size distribution, and flowability, among other factors, depend on the powder production process and directly influence the processing parameters and physical characteristics of the parts built by AM. This systematic review presents different concepts involving L-PBF and DLD manufacturing and the application of metal powders. The methods used to produce and characterize metal powders and the modification techniques to improve their processability by AM are detailed and discussed. Environmental and health risks are also presented, and safety measures that must be considered while handling metal powders. Some key topics requiring attention for further development are highlighted. Graphical abstract

Abstract:
The additive manufacturing process creates objects directly by stacking layers of material on each other until the required product is obtained. The application of additive manufacturing technology for teaching and research purposes is still limited and unpopular in developing countries, due to costs and lack of accessibility. In this study, an extruding-based 3D printing additive manufacturing technology was employed to design and construct a low-cost-high-accessibility 3D printing machine to manufacture plastic objects. The machine was designed using SolidWorks 2020 version with a 10 × 10 × 10 cm3 build volume. The fabrication was carried out using locally available materials, such as PVC pipes for the frame, plywood for the bed, and Zinc Oxide plaster for the bed surface. Repetier firmware was the operating environment for devices running on the computer operating system. Cura was used as the slicing software. The fabricated machine was tested, and the printer produced 3D components with desired structural dimensions. The fabricated 3D printer was used to manufacture some plastic objects using PLA filament. The recommended distance between the nozzle tip and the bed is 0.1 mm. The constructed 3D printer is affordable and accessible, especially in developing nations where 3D printing applications are limited and unpopular.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of titanium or titanium alloys allows fabrication of geometrically more complex and, possibly, individualized implants or osteosynthesis products and could thus improve the outcome of medical treatments considerably. However, insufficient LPBF process parameters can result in substantial porosity, decreasing mechanical properties and requiring post-treatment. Furthermore, texturized parts with anisotropic properties are usually obtained after LPBF processing, limiting their usage in medical applications. The present study addresses both: first, a design of experiments is used in order to establish a set of optimized process parameters and a process window for LPBF printing of small commercially pure (CP) titanium parts with minimized volume porosity. Afterward, the first results on the development of a biocompatible titanium alloy designed for LPBF processing of medical implants with improved solidification and more isotropic properties are presented on the basis of conventionally melted alloys. This development was performed on the basis of Ti-0.44O-0.5Fe-0.08C-0.4Si-0.1Au, a near-α alloy presented by the authors for medical applications and conventional manufacturing, with yttrium and boron additions as additional growth restriction solutes. In terms of LPBF processing of CP titanium grade 1 powder, a high relative density of approximately 99.9% was obtained in the as-printed state of the volume of a small cubical sample by using optimized laser power, scanning speed, and hatch distance in combination with a rotating scanning pattern. Moreover, tensile specimens processed with these volume settings and tested in the as-printed milled state exhibited a high average yield and ultimate tensile strength of approximately 663 and 747 N/mm2, respectively, combined with a high average ductility of approximately 24%. X-ray diffraction results suggest anisotropic mechanical properties, which are, however, less pronounced in terms of the tested specimens. Regarding alloy development, the results show that yttrium additions lead to a considerable microstructure refinement but have to be limited due to the occurrence of a large amount of precipitations and a supposed higher propensity for the formation of long columnar prior β-grains. However, phase/texture and microstructure analyses indicate that Ti-0.44O-0.5Fe-0.08C-0.4Si-0.1Au-0.1B-0.1Y is a promising candidate to achieve lower anisotropy during LPBF processing, but further investigations on LPBF printing and Y2O3 formation are necessary.

The growing demand for more materials available for the LPBF-process, in particular high-strength aluminum alloys, is evident in the market. In the present work, a systematic investigation of the processability of aluminum 6182 series alloys, using LPBF, was carried out. For this purpose, the influence of process parameters, especially of enhanced preheating by heating the substrate plate during the LPBF process, on the microstructure of EN AW 6182 specimens was studied. Experiments were conducted at different preheating temperatures always using the same d-optimal design-of-experiments, the laser power, scanning speed, hatch distance, and laser focus position being varied over a wide range. It was found that the preheating temperature has the strongest impact on hot cracking. Higher temperatures result in a significantly reduced number of hot cracks in the microstructure. Moreover, an equiaxed microstructure of the specimens manufactured can be observed at preheating temperatures of 500 °C. In addition to the preheating temperature, the achievable part density is most strongly affected by the laser focus position and the laser power, whereas the hatch distance shows no discernible impact on the part density. Furthermore, neither the hatch distance nor the laser focus position shows any significant effect on hot cracking. In combination with the optimal scanning parameters, crack-free parts with a fully equiaxed grain structure and densities > 99.0% can be manufactured via LPBF at a preheating temperature of 500 °C.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) is a layerwise production process that creates three-dimensional objects according to a digital model. This technology has demonstrated to be a promising alternative to conventional manufacturing methods for various industrial sectors, such as aerospace, automotive, biomedical, and energy. AM offers several advantages, like design flexibility, material efficiency, functional integration, and rapid prototyping. As regards metal parts, conventional AM techniques using infrared laser sources face some limitations in processing high-reflectivity and high-conductivity materials or alloys, such as aluminum, copper, gold, and silver. These materials have low absorption of infrared radiation, which results in unstable and shallow melt pools, poor surface quality, and high porosity. To overcome these challenges, green and blue laser sources have been proposed for AM processes. This review provides an overview of the recent developments and applications of green and blue laser sources for powder bed fusion of copper and its alloys, focusing on the effects of process parameters on the melt pool dynamics, microstructure formation, and thermal and electrical properties of the fabricated parts. This review also presents the main applications of AM of copper and its alloys together with potential opportunities for future developments.

The excerpt describes an open-architecture DTU LPBF controller centered on a Teensy 3.6 with a 180 MHz ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller. It uses direct memory access (DMA), timer interrupts, and a circular command buffer so scanner and laser operation can continue while commands are received and processed. The scanner interface is the XY2-100 protocol: a 20-bit, 2 MHz asynchronous digital protocol using four differential pairs for clock, synchronization, and two mirror-position data channels. This article has 4 citations.

The NIST powder spreading testbed (PST) is a compact, two-axis powder-spreading apparatus intended to reproduce key aspects of commercial laser powder bed fusion while reducing powder requirements and fitting inside an environmentally controlled chamber. Its 200 mm × 100 mm baseplate is smaller than a typical 250 mm square commercial platform; the reduced width is justified by an assumed continuity of spreading physics along the recoater blade beyond a characteristic length scale. A Newport XPS Q8 controller drives the recoater’s linear motion and the Z-axis baseplate height. The recoater carriage travels on a ball-screw linear slide, and the system includes limit switches, a viewing glass for side imaging, a catchment area for overflow, and a fixed, inspected baseplate. Powder heaps are generated either with a stencil, which is convenient for single-layer spreading and creates a narrower heap, or with a rotating steel-cylinder apparatus, which is better suited to multilayer spreading but produces a more distributed heap. The excerpt does not provide quantitative definitions or measurement procedures for spreadability metrics such as coverage, packing fraction, or surface roughness. It also does not discuss inserts or hopper-feed designs; it only explains that the PST omits a commercial-style powder collection mechanism to save space and avoid additional motion systems.

Particle tracks are extracted as frame number and x-y position, then used to calculate velocity and acceleration. The machine includes a build piston, piston-fed powder supply, and compliant-blade recoating mechanism, with these functions actuated by industrial-automation-grade servo motors. The laser scan head is suspended on a boom above the enclosure and delivers light from a 500 W, 1.075 µm SPI redPOWER qube single-mode fiber laser. The laser has 82 mrad beam divergence and is paired with a 250 mm collimator, producing a 19.5 mm beam diameter. {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a comparison table of open-architecture / custom LPBF research testbeds with columns: System Name, Institution, Laser (type/power/wavelength), Scanner, Build Volume/Area, Recoater, Chamber/Gas, Monitoring, and Key Lessons. Include rows for:
1. NIST AMMT: 500W (later 195W reported in datasets) 1070nm fiber laser, galvo scanner with SiC mirrors, 100x100mm build area, argon, FPGA control, coaxial melt-pool camera (Mikrotron EOSens 3CL1), layer camera (Basler acA3800-10gm), SimpleAM software, XY2-100 protocol at 100kHz
2. Bidare et al. (Heriot-Watt): 400W 1070nm SPI fiber laser, Raylase MS-II-14 scanner with 163mm f-theta, ~30x30mm build area/10mm depth, silicon cord compliant spreader at ~10mm/s, Perspex chamber 350x230x220mm, gas cross-flow with water bath exhaust, LabVIEW control
3. DTU Open AM (Andersen/Kjer/Pedersen): 250W SPI laser, Sunny Galvo SG S9320D digital scanner (20mm aperture, <0.4ms step), XY2-100 protocol, Teensy 3.6 ARM Cortex-M4 controller, open-source firmware, coaxial NIR photodiode, O2/flow sensors
4. MIT/Hart testbed (Penny et al.): 500W 1075nm SPI redPOWER qube, Thorlabs QS20XY galvo, compliant blade recoater, piston-fed powder, NI-cRIO-9039 control, MWIR camera (IRC806HS), 60mm lid clearance
5. Aconity Mini: 190W 1064nm Nd:YAG, cylindrical bed Ø140mm x 200mm, wiper rake recoater, argon atmosphere, modular open platform
6. DAMX (Sheffield/Aydin): Multiple lasers (450nm/915nm/1064nm options, 200W SPI fiber with galvo), Ø125mm x 170mm build, argon <0.1% O2, optional vacuum, heating to 1200°C"}

{"answer": "# Design and Customization of a Sub-$60k Desktop LPBF Machine for Aluminium Alloy Screening: A Literature-Based Review

## 1. Open-Source and Open-Architecture LPBF Research Testbeds

The literature documents several custom and open-architecture LPBF platforms that serve as design references for a research-grade machine.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**NIST AMMT/TEMPS.** The NIST Additive Manufacturing Metrology Testbed uses a 500 W fiber laser (with published datasets at 195 W) at 1070 nm, directed by a galvanometer scanner through SiC mirrors over a 100 × 100 mm build area (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046). The sealed chamber (1750 × 1200 × 780 mm) is evacuated and backfilled with argon at 300 L/min flow (pqac-00000047). FPGA-based acquisition controls scanner motion and laser power; in-situ monitoring includes a coaxial Mikrotron EOSens 3CL1 melt-pool camera at 10,000 fps and a Basler acA3800-10gm layer camera (pqac-00000047). Scan commands use the XY2-100 protocol at 100 kHz (10 µs timesteps), with each row containing X, Y, power, and trigger columns (pqac-00000050). A critical lesson was that scattered laser light caused a folding mirror to reach approximately 275 °C and its silver coating to fail; recommended mitigations included forced-air cooling, baffling, and use of silicon mirror substrates (pqac-00000000).

**Bidare et al. (Heriot-Watt).** This compact, portable platform uses a 400 W, 1070 nm SPI single-mode fiber laser with a Raylase MS-II-14 scanner and 163 mm f-theta lens, achieving a ~50 µm spot (pqac-00000004). The build area is approximately 30 × 30 mm with 10 mm depth—deliberately small to minimize powder consumption (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000007). A key lesson was that rigid tungsten-carbide knife and cylindrical spreaders jammed, so a 3 mm-diameter silicon cord was adopted as a compliant recoater at ~10 mm/s spreading speed with a 50 µm gap (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000008). The detachable Perspex chamber (350 × 230 × 220 mm) uses gas cross-flow with exhaust bubbled through a water bath to trap nanoparticles (pqac-00000005). The system achieved >99% part density and demonstrated that slow recoating dominated build time rather than laser scanning (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008).

**DTU Open Additive Manufacturing Initiative.** Andersen, Kjer, and Pedersen developed an open-source unified controller based on a Teensy 3.6 (180 MHz ARM Cortex-M4), using DMA and timer interrupts for deterministic scanner-laser synchronization (pqac-00000009). The scanner interface is the XY2-100 protocol—a 20-bit, 2 MHz asynchronous digital protocol providing 16-bit (65,536-level) position resolution per axis (pqac-00000009). They use a Sunny Galvo SG S9320D digital scanner with 20 mm aperture, <0.4 ms small-step response, <8 µrad repeatability, and >99.9% linearity (pqac-00000012). The laser is a 250 W SPI fiber laser controlled via a 0–10 V analog signal (10-bit DAC, 0.24 W increment) with PWM modulation up to 100 kHz (pqac-00000011). The open-source firmware supports PID gas-flow control via VFD pumps, O₂ sensing, coaxial NIR photodiode monitoring, and three configurable sensor inputs (0–10 V or 4–20 mA) (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). The platform operates three LPBF/SLS systems and avoids proprietary lock-in (pqac-00000014).

**MIT/Hart Testbed.** Penny et al. built a bespoke platform around a 500 W, 1.075 µm SPI redPOWER qube single-mode fiber laser with a 250 mm collimator producing a 19.5 mm beam, scanned by a Thorlabs QS20XY galvanometer (pqac-00000072, pqac-00000073). It features servo-actuated compliant-blade recoating, piston-fed powder supply, and only 60 mm clearance between the build plate and enclosure lid (pqac-00000072). Automation uses an NI cRIO-9039 on a 10 µs timebase; monitoring includes a high-speed MWIR camera (IRCameras IRC806HS, 640 × 512 InSb, 1–5 µm, ~50 µm resolution) through a CaF₂ protective window (pqac-00000073).

**Aconity Mini.** This commercial research platform uses a 190 W, 1064 nm Nd:YAG laser with adjustable focus over a cylindrical bed of Ø140 mm × 200 mm height; powder is delivered by a wiper rake from a manually filled reservoir, with argon backfill (pqac-00000002).

**DAMX (Sheffield).** This multi-wavelength platform supports interchangeable 450 nm, 915 nm, and 1064 nm laser heads (200 W SPI fiber + galvo with 70 µm spot), a Ø125 × 170 mm build envelope, layer thicknesses down to 10 µm, conductive preheating to 1200 °C, and a CFD-designed argon circulation maintaining <0.1% O₂ with optional vacuum below 10 mbar (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003).

---

## 2. Powder Spreading: Recoater Design, Speed, Layer Thickness, and Spreadability

**Blade vs. Roller.** A direct comparison of single-layer packing densities found: non-rotating roller 45.39%, rotating roller 43.09%, chamfer recoater 42.21%, and straight blade 30.30% (pqac-00000065). The non-rotating roller produced the most uniform layer and fewest empty patches, while the straight blade suffered from point contact, particle dragging, roughness, and cavities (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000065). However, at very thin layers (e.g., 70 µm), rollers can produce the *lowest* density due to particle jamming (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019). Counter-rotating rollers at high rates (>4.8π rad/s) harmed bed stability, while forward rotation improved packing density and surface morphology (pqac-00000015). Among blade geometries, wide-nose (NB) blades outperformed sharp-edge (IB) blades because the rounded leading edge creates a compression zone (pqac-00000070).

**Compliant recoaters.** Bidare et al. found that rigid metal spreaders jammed; a 3 mm silicon cord successfully spread powder at 50 µm gap (pqac-00000004). The MIT/Hart system also uses a servo-actuated compliant blade (pqac-00000072). Flexible polymer blades accommodate surface irregularities and improve robustness versus rigid blades (pqac-00000020).

**Recoater speed and layer thickness.** Typical LPBF layer thicknesses are 20–100 µm, with 20–40 µm common for high-resolution aerospace/biomedical applications (pqac-00000021). Reported recoater speeds range from 10 mm/s (Bidare) through 25–75 mm/s to 500 mm/s (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000015). An optimal speed of 250 mm/s was identified for PA12 within a 125–500 mm/s range (pqac-00000015). Lower speeds generally improve packing density and uniformity but increase build time (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020).

**Particle size effects.** A critical particle radius of ~21.8 µm was reported: reducing from 84.7 to 61.6 µm improved flowability, but reducing from 17.4 to 12.2 µm worsened it due to van der Waals forces (pqac-00000017). Powder cohesion—especially below 100 µm—promotes clustering and reduces flowability (pqac-00000021). For the user's 15–63 µm range, particles near the fine end may cause flow issues.

**Minimizing powder consumption.** Bidare's ~30 × 30 mm build area consumed very small powder quantities (pqac-00000007). The NIST powder spreading testbed uses a 200 × 100 mm baseplate (reduced width justified by scaling arguments), with stencil-based or rotating-cylinder heap delivery rather than large piston reservoirs (pqac-00000058). The Aconity Mini's cylindrical Ø140 mm bed and manual reservoir also reduce waste (pqac-00000002). Piston-fed designs (MIT/Hart) offer precise dosing but require the reservoir volume to match or exceed the build volume (pqac-00000072).

---

## 3. Inert-Gas Environment for Aluminium Alloys

**O₂ requirements.** For LPBF of aluminium alloys, chambers are purged to below 0.1% O₂ (~1000 ppm); operating levels are typically a few hundred ppm (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029). Even at 0.1–0.2% O₂, thin oxide layers form on aluminium, disrupting melt-pool stability, causing balling, reducing wettability, and promoting lack-of-fusion porosity (pqac-00000026). Residual O₂ below 500 ppm can still react with aluminium and titanium to form oxides (pqac-00000028). For reactive alloys like Al-Mg-Sc/Zr, targeting <200 ppm is prudent.

**Purge strategies.** The NIST AMMT uses evacuate-and-backfill with argon or nitrogen (pqac-00000045). The DAMX supports optional vacuum below 10 mbar before argon backfill (pqac-00000003). Vacuum-purge-backfill is more effective at removing moisture and achieving low initial O₂ than flow-through purging alone (pqac-00000023). Humidity must also be removed from powder and chamber, as laser interaction can split moisture into hydrogen (causing porosity in aluminium) and oxygen (pqac-00000044).

**Cross-flow velocity.** For effective spatter and plume removal, a minimum cross-flow velocity of approximately 2.0 m/s is needed; below this, spatters rise vertically and vapor plumes are poorly removed, causing a sharp decrease in melt-pool penetration (pqac-00000025). In a commercial EOS M290, maximum cross-flow reaches ~3.5 m/s near the inlet nozzle (25 mm above the platform) and ~2 m/s at mid-plate (pqac-00000051). At 4 m/s nominal inlet velocity, volumetric flow was ~300 L/min (~18 m³/h) (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000056). Flow is non-uniform across the plate—highest near the inlet, lowest near the outlet—and is affected by the recoater body (pqac-00000056).

**Nozzle design.** The EOS M290 uses dual inlets: an upper inlet near the chamber roof (preventing recirculation toward the laser window) and a lower nozzle near the build plate. The standard nozzle has many small circular holes leading to larger channels; the grid nozzle uses rectangular channels with a bottom row projecting gas downward (pqac-00000052). The NIST AMMT nozzle is an array of 3.2 mm-diameter circular channels with a length-to-diameter ratio of ~15.5 (pqac-00000052). Bidare's system uses simple side-inlet ports reversible for gases heavier or lighter than air, with exhaust through a water bath (pqac-00000005).

**Gas consumption and filtration.** At 300 L/min recirculating flow with fresh-gas top-up when O₂ exceeds 0.2%, consumption depends on chamber leak rate and build duration (pqac-00000024). For a small desktop chamber (~30–50 L volume), initial purge requires 3–5 chamber volumes (~100–250 L) and steady-state consumption is modest if leak-tight. Bidare's water-bath exhaust captures nanoparticles (pqac-00000005); commercial machines use HEPA-class filters in recirculating loops.

---

## 4. Beam Delivery: Galvanometer Scanner vs. Gantry

**Galvanometer + f-theta lens.** This is the standard LPBF beam-delivery architecture. Galvo mirrors change position on microsecond timescales (pqac-00000033). The Sunny Galvo SG S9320D has a 20 mm aperture, <0.4 ms small-step response, ±12.5° scan angle, >99.9% linearity, <8 µrad repeatability, <50 ppm/°C scale drift, and <15 µrad/°C zero drift (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000036). The XY2-100 protocol provides 16-bit position space per axis at 2 MHz update rate (pqac-00000009). Typical f-theta focal lengths are 163 mm (Bidare, pqac-00000004) to 250+ mm; voice-coil dynamic focusing is an alternative that avoids the cost and beam-distortion issues of large f-theta lenses (pqac-00000034). Spot sizes of 50–100 µm are standard; the NIST AMMT achieves ~60 × 48 µm (D4σ) (pqac-00000046), while DAMX reports 70 µm (pqac-00000003).

**Gantry-based systems.** XY gantry motion is used in some DPM/DAM systems but is fundamentally slower than galvo scanning for LPBF. No quantitative gantry acceleration data for LPBF were found in the reviewed literature. Galvo scanning at speeds of 500–2100 mm/s is routine for aluminium (pqac-00000030); gantry systems would be limited to <100 mm/s by inertia.

**Fiber laser for aluminium.** AlSi10Mg has very low absorptivity at 1070 nm—approximately 9% (pqac-00000030)—and 5–10% at 1064 nm for powder (pqac-00000031). Near-full density was obtained using 300 W at 500 mm/s, while higher productivity was achieved at 900 W / 2100 mm/s (pqac-00000030). For a desktop machine, 300–500 W at 1070 nm is the practical minimum for aluminium processing. Blue lasers (450 nm) offer ~15% absorptivity but are currently more expensive and lower power (pqac-00000031).

**Protective window contamination.** The upper gas inlet directs flow to prevent process byproducts from reaching the laser lens or protective window (pqac-00000051). The MIT/Hart system uses a CaF₂ protective window (pqac-00000073). Back-reflection from aluminium is a serious concern; the NIST AMMT experienced coating failure on optical elements due to back-reflected/scattered laser power (pqac-00000000).

---

## 5. Controls and Electronics

**Scanner protocols.** The XY2-100 is the most common industrial galvanometer protocol: a 20-bit, 2 MHz asynchronous digital interface using four differential pairs (clock, sync, X-data, Y-data), with each control word containing 3 mode bits, 16 position bits, and 1 parity bit (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). The NIST AMMT uses XYPT command files at 100 kHz (pqac-00000050).

**Laser modulation.** The DTU system provides 0–10 V analog power control (10-bit DAC, 0.24 W increments for a 250 W laser) plus a 24 V PWM enable signal supporting CW or pulsed operation up to 100 kHz (pqac-00000011). The Forhad thesis describes a similar architecture with 0–10 V analog (representing 0–1000 W) and 8-bit digital laser interfaces (pqac-00000032).

**Open-source control.** The DTU Unified Systems Controller firmware is open-source, runs on Teensy 3.6, and coordinates scanner, laser, gas flow, motors, beam expander, and sensor inputs (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014). NIST uses SimpleAM (SAM) for scan-path generation (pqac-00000050). PySLM is an open-source Python library for scan-path planning. The Reiff et al. group demonstrated learning feedforward control via an interface card to laser and galvo using XY2-100 (pqac-00000009).

**In-situ monitoring.** Common sensors in custom LPBF machines include: coaxial melt-pool cameras (Mikrotron EOSens 3CL1 at NIST, pqac-00000047), layer-wise cameras (Basler acA3800-10gm, pqac-00000047), MWIR cameras (IRC806HS at MIT, pqac-00000073), coaxial NIR photodiodes (DTU, pqac-00000009), pyrometers, and O₂/flow sensors. The DTU controller provides three configurable sensor inputs accepting 0–10 V or 4–20 mA signals (pqac-00000009).

---

## 6. Safety

**Laser safety.** A custom LPBF machine with a ≥200 W Class 4 fiber laser must comply with IEC 60825-1 (classification and requirements) and IEC 60825-4 (laser guards) internationally, or ANSI Z136.1 in the United States. The system must be a fully enclosed Class 1 enclosure with safety interlocks on all access panels, a laser-safe viewing window (OD ≥ 6+ at 1070 nm), emergency stop, and key switch. The NIST AMMT and MIT/Hart systems both use sealed enclosures with protective windows (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000073). Back-reflection from aluminium requires particular attention: an isolator on the laser output fiber and baffling/cooling of scanner optics are essential (pqac-00000000).

**Combustible metal powder handling.** NFPA 484 (Standard for Combustible Metals) and NFPA 654 (Prevention of Fire and Dust Explosions) are the governing U.S. standards (pqac-00000039). Aluminium powder is specifically identified as presenting fire and explosion hazards (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000043). Key controls include: inert-atmosphere processing, elimination of ignition sources, spark-resistant tooling, anti-static equipment, wet separators or passivated filters for exhaust (Bidare used a water bath, pqac-00000005), full-face respirators and full-body PPE, segregated powder-handling rooms with signage and access controls, anti-static vacuum cleaners for spills, and "sticky rooms" for personnel decontamination (pqac-00000037).

**Nanoparticle hazards.** LPBF laser-material interaction generates respirable nanoparticles and agglomerates that are deposited on internal machine surfaces and can be carried into offices, break rooms, and other non-production areas on clothing and equipment (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000041). Correctly functioning exhaust-air or recirculating-air filtration (HEPA) is essential; faulty filtration was identified as a source of internal contamination (pqac-00000041). Personal exposures during machine opening and cleaning can exceed stationary measurements because workers lean into the build chamber (pqac-00000038).

**Moisture.** Humidity must be removed from the chamber and powder because laser interaction can split moisture into hydrogen (which dissolves in molten aluminium and produces gas porosity) and oxygen (which forms oxides) (pqac-00000044).

---

## 7. Ranked Design Recommendations for a Sub-$60k Custom Desktop LPBF for Aluminium Alloy Screening

Based on the literature reviewed, the following design choices are ranked by strength of evidence and suitability for the stated application (small batches of 15–63 µm ultrasonically atomized aluminium powder, good spreadability, safety, automation, minimal powder volume, high-purity inert gas):

1. **Small build area (~50 × 50 mm) with piston-fed or hopper-fed powder delivery.** The Bidare system demonstrated that a ~30 × 30 mm build area uses minimal powder and achieves >99% density (pqac-00000006). A 50 × 50 mm plate is a reasonable compromise between coupon variety and powder conservation. A small piston reservoir or gravity hopper above the recoater minimizes dead volume compared to large side-feed pistons.

2. **Compliant-blade or wide-nose-blade recoater at 50–150 mm/s.** Rigid metal blades jam with fine powders; compliant recoaters (silicon cord, rubber, or polymer blade) solved this problem in multiple testbeds (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000072). Wide-nose blades produce higher packing than sharp-edge blades (pqac-00000070). A speed of ~100 mm/s balances packing density and build time (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017). Layer thickness of 30–50 µm suits the 15–63 µm PSD.

3. **300–500 W single-mode fiber laser at 1070 nm.** AlSi10Mg absorptivity is only ~9% at this wavelength, requiring ≥300 W for near-full-density parts at standard scan speeds (pqac-00000030). A 500 W SPI redPOWER qube (used at MIT and NIST) costs ~$15–25k and provides headroom. An optical isolator is mandatory to protect against aluminium back-reflection (pqac-00000000).

4. **Galvanometer scanner with XY2-100 digital protocol and f-theta lens.** The Sunny Galvo SG S9320D (~$3–5k) or Raylase MS-II-14 are proven choices with <0.4 ms step response, <8 µrad repeatability, and 20 mm aperture (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000004). A 163–254 mm f-theta lens provides 50–80 µm spots over the small build area. XY2-100 is the standard, non-proprietary scanner interface (pqac-00000009).

5. **Vacuum-purge-backfill chamber with recirculating argon cross-flow ≥2 m/s.** For aluminium, target <500 ppm O₂ (operating) with a <0.1% (1000 ppm) hard interlock (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000025). Initial vacuum evacuation removes moisture and achieves low O₂ faster than flow-through purging (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000023). A small chamber (~30 L) requires modest gas; recirculating flow at 2–3 m/s with a HEPA filter and O₂ sensor maintains atmosphere quality (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000051). A zirconia O₂ sensor (ppm-level) and dew-point sensor are recommended.

6. **Open-source embedded controller (Teensy 3.6 or equivalent ARM).** The DTU Unified Systems Controller provides deterministic XY2-100 galvo control, 0–10 V laser power, PWM modulation, PID gas-flow control, and sensor acquisition on a single low-cost microcontroller (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011). Its open-source firmware is extensible and avoids vendor lock-in. Alternatively, an NI cRIO provides industrial-grade determinism but at higher cost (~$5–10k vs. ~$100 for Teensy) (pqac-00000073).

7. **Coaxial photodiode or camera for melt-pool monitoring.** A coaxial NIR photodiode (as used at DTU, pqac-00000009) is the lowest-cost in-situ sensor (~$200–500) and provides real-time melt-pool intensity feedback. A coaxial camera (Mikrotron or similar) adds spatial resolution but costs $5–15k (pqac-00000047).

8. **Full Class 1 laser enclosure with NFPA 484 powder controls.** The enclosure must have interlocked panels per IEC 60825-4, OD 6+ viewing window, emergency stop, and key switch. Aluminium powder handling requires inert-atmosphere glove-box or sealed transfer, wet separator or water-bath exhaust, HEPA filtration, anti-static tooling, full-face respirator and full-body PPE, and segregated handling area (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000005).

9. **Gas-knife or cross-flow nozzle with dual-inlet design.** A lower nozzle array near the build plate (3–5 mm diameter channels, L/D ~15) provides laminar cross-flow for spatter removal, while an upper inlet prevents recirculation toward the laser window (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000051).

10. **Stepper/servo-actuated Z-axis and recoater carriage with ball-screw drives.** The NIST PST uses a Newport XPS controller with ball-screw linear slides (pqac-00000058). Industrial servo motors provide smooth motion and precise layer-height control; the Bidare system uses stepper motors with fine-pitch screws (pqac-00000004).

**Estimated cost breakdown (approximate):** 500 W fiber laser $15–25k; galvo scanner + f-theta $3–8k; controller electronics $1–3k; linear stages and motors $2–5k; chamber fabrication $3–5k; gas system (valves, sensors, filter) $2–4k; enclosure and safety $3–5k; optics and protective window $1–3k; miscellaneous (wiring, software development) $2–5k. **Total: approximately $32–63k**, consistent with the sub-$60k target when component choices are optimized.
